title: Indifference means a real power to act or not, which remains even after the agent has decided
source_text: XXVIII. Itaque libertas hominis in agendo non male constituitur in quadam ejus circa actus suos indeterminatione & indifferentia. Verum observandum est per istam indifferentiam non intelligi, ut quidam suspicari videntur, statum ancipitem hominis fluctuantis, necdum certi quo vergat atque inclinet; sed veram potestatem agendi, vel non agendi, & actionem suam sic, vel sic instituendi; quae manet etiam in eo, qui proprio judicio atque electione se ad actiones has, aut illas determinavit, & apud quem certum & constitutum est hoc & non aliud agere.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore the liberty of man in acting is not badly placed in a certain indetermination & indifference of his about his acts. But it is to be observed that by that indifference is not understood, as some seem to suspect, the doubtful state of a man wavering, and not yet certain where he may turn and incline; but a true power of acting, or not acting, & of ordering his action thus, or thus; which remains even in him, who by his own judgement and election has determined himself to these, or those actions, & with whom it is certain & settled to do this & not another thing.
pass_b_english: So it is not wrong to place man's freedom in acting in a certain openness and indifference he has toward his acts.

Note, however, that this indifference does not mean, as some seem to suppose, the uncertain state of a man who wavers and has not yet settled which way to turn and lean. It means a real power to act or not act, and to arrange his action one way or another. That power remains even in someone who by his own judgement and choice has settled on these actions or those, and for whom it is fixed and decided to do this and nothing else.

choices.why: The technical sense is defined here as a standing power to act or not, not a state of wavering; the term is kept.
